lesson.title: What is Physics?
lesson.introduction: Physics is the branch of science that studies matter, energy, and how they interact.
lesson.explanation:
Physics explains why objects move, why the sky is blue, how electricity works, and how machines function. It uses measurement, experiment and mathematics.

Length, mass and time are the three fundamental quantities. The unit of length is the metre (m), mass is the kilogram (kg), and time is the second (s). Physics depends on accurate measurement. A measurement includes a number and a unit.
keyPoints: Every measurement has a value and a unit.

lesson.title: Introduction to Waves
lesson.introduction: A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without permanently transferring matter.
lesson.explanation:
When you drop a stone into a calm pond, ripples spread outward. The water itself does not travel across the pond; instead, energy is passed from one water particle to the next. This is a wave.

Waves can be grouped in two ways:

1. By how they move: A transverse wave oscillates perpendicular to the direction of travel (light, water waves, waves on a string). A longitudinal wave oscillates parallel to the direction of travel (sound).
2. By whether they need a medium: Mechanical waves (sound, water, seismic) need a material medium. Electromagnetic waves (light, radio) can travel through a vacuum.

Key quantities:
- Wavelength (λ): the distance between two identical points on consecutive waves, measured in metres.
- Frequency (f): the number of complete waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
- Speed (v): how fast the wave travels, in metres per second (m/s).

The wave equation relates them: v = f × λ.

Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position. It tells us the energy of the wave: a larger amplitude carries more energy.
keyPoints: A wave transfers energy, not matter.
Transverse waves: vibration is perpendicular to travel (light).
Longitudinal waves: vibration is parallel to travel (sound).
v = f × λ, where v is speed, f is frequency, λ is wavelength.
Amplitude shows the energy carried by the wave.

examples.title: Calculating wavelength
examples.problem: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and travels at 300 m/s. Find its wavelength.
examples.solution: v = fλ so λ = v/f = 300/50 = 6 m

questions.prompt: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and travels at 300 m/s. Calculate its wavelength.
questions.expectedWorking:
v = f × λ
λ = v / f
λ = 300 / 50
λ = 6 m
questions.explanation: Rearrange v = fλ for λ: λ = v/f = 300/50 = 6 m. The values were substituted correctly.

topics.description: Production and properties of sound, echoes and applications.

lesson.title: Sound as a Longitudinal Wave
lesson.introduction: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies and travels as a longitudinal mechanical wave.
lesson.explanation:
Strike a tuning fork and it vibrates. These vibrations push and pull the air particles, creating compressions (particles squeezed together) and rarefactions (particles spread apart). The disturbance travels outward at roughly 330–340 m/s in air.

Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because it needs particles to carry the disturbance. It travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases.

The pitch of a sound depends on its frequency: high frequency means high pitch. Loudness depends on the amplitude: bigger amplitude means louder sound. The quality (timbre) distinguishes two sounds of the same pitch and loudness, like a piano and a guitar playing the same note.

An echo is a repeated sound caused by reflection of sound waves off a hard surface. Paramedics use ultrasound to see inside the body; sailors use echo-sounding to measure depth.
keyPoints: Sound is a longitudinal, mechanical wave.
It cannot travel through a vacuum.
Speed of sound in air is about 340 m/s.

questions.explanation: Sound travels fastest in solids because particles are tightly packed and transfer vibrations quickly. It cannot travel in a vacuum.

questions.prompt: The pitch of a sound depends on its
questions.explanation: Pitch depends on frequency — higher frequency gives higher pitch.

questions.prompt: A boy shouts near a cliff and hears the echo after 3 s. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, how far away is the cliff?
questions.expectedWorking:
Total distance travelled by sound (to cliff and back) = v × t = 340 × 3 = 1020 m
Cliff distance = 1020 / 2 = 510 m
questions.explanation: The sound goes to the cliff and returns, so the distance is half of (340 × 3) = 510 m.

questions.prompt: Loudness of a sound increases when its ___ increases.
questions.explanation: Loudness is related to the amplitude (energy) of the sound wave.
